newsitem.title: USA: SBC presses ahead with long-distance plans.
newsitem.headline: SBC presses ahead with long-distance plans.

text.p: SBC Communications Inc., whose merger talks with AT&T Corp. collapsed last week, will press ahead with plans to offer long-distance service despite regulatory setbacks, a company spokesman said on Monday.

The San Antonio-based Baby Bell is preparing an appeal to last week's decision by federal regulators blocking its bid to offer long-distance service in Oklahoma and will seek approval by the end of the year to add long-distance calling in six other states where it operates, spokesman Larry Solomon said.
"We still intend on getting long-distance business in the seven states where we provide local calling," said Solomon. He declined to comment on reports the company broke off merger talks with AT&T.

Sources last week said talks on a $50 billion merger between SBC and AT&T collapsed following sharp criticism from regulators. Both companies have declined to comment on reports of merger talks initiated two months ago by SBC Chairman Edward Whitacre.

SBC's bid to offer long-distance service to its customers in Oklahoma was rejected Thursday by the Federal Communications Commission, which said SBC had failed to adequately open its monopoly market in the state to competitors.

SBC contends its service territory has been opened to competitors -- including long-distance providers and cable television companies -- but that competition has failed to emerge because rivals have only offered service in metropolitan areas.

The Baby Bell has spent about $1.2 billion and dedicated about 4,000 of its 110,000 employees to solve technical and marketing issues involved in opening the local monopolies to competition, Solomon said.

"We've opened the door, but the problem is only a few competitors have walked through the door," he said. SBC operates local calling networks in California, Texas, Oklahoma, Nevada, Arkansas, Kansas and Missouri.

The Baby Bells have been barred from entering the $80 billion-a-year national long-distance market since the 1984 breakup of AT&T, and face increased competition for their share of the $100 billion-a-year local-calling business.

Separately, AT&T said Monday it cut long-distance rates by 5 percent on daytime calls and 15 percent on night and weekend calls following an FCC order that will lower access fees the long-distance carriers pay to local telephone companies.
